answer:
Rosenmund reduction is the reduction of an acyl chloride to the corresponding aldehyde by hydrogen over a palladium catalyst supported on barium sulfate (section 12.4.3). The catalyst is deliberately poisoned so that the reduction stops at the aldehyde stage and does not go on to the alcohol.

\(\mathrm{R-COCl} + \mathrm{H_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Pd/BaSO_4}} \mathrm{R-CHO} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

For example, ethanoyl chloride gives ethanal :

\(\mathrm{CH_3-COCl} + \mathrm{H_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Pd/BaSO_4}} \mathrm{CH_3-CHO} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

and benzoyl chloride gives benzaldehyde :

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-COCl} + \mathrm{H_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Pd/BaSO_4}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-CHO} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

In Gatterman-Koch formylation benzene, or a substituted benzene, is treated with carbon monoxide and hydrogen chloride under high pressure in presence of anhydrous aluminium chloride, cuprous chloride being used along with it. A \(\mathrm{-CHO}\) group is introduced directly into the ring, so benzene gives benzaldehyde (section 12.4.3).

\(\mathrm{C_6H_6} + \mathrm{CO} + \mathrm{HCl} \xrightarrow[\text{high pressure}]{\text{anhyd. } \mathrm{AlCl_3}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-CHO} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

With toluene the ring-activating methyl group is ortho- and para-directing and the para product predominates, so 4-methylbenzaldehyde is obtained :

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-CH_3} + \mathrm{CO} + \mathrm{HCl} \xrightarrow[\text{high pressure}]{\text{anhyd. } \mathrm{AlCl_3}} \mathrm{4\text{-}CH_3-C_6H_4-CHO} + \mathrm{HCl}\)
twin: Name the product obtained by reacting toluene with carbon monoxide and hydrogen chloride in presence of anhydrous aluminium chloride.

answer:
Rosenmund reduction converts an acyl chloride into the aldehyde with the same number of carbon atoms. Hydrogen is passed over the acyl chloride in presence of palladium supported on barium sulfate; the catalyst is poisoned so that the aldehyde formed is not reduced further to the alcohol (section 12.4.3).

\(\mathrm{R-COCl} + \mathrm{H_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Pd/BaSO_4}} \mathrm{R-CHO} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

For example, benzoyl chloride gives benzaldehyde :

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-COCl} + \mathrm{H_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Pd/BaSO_4}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-CHO} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

Gatterman-Koch formylation introduces a \(\mathrm{-CHO}\) group directly into an aromatic ring. The arene is treated under high pressure with carbon monoxide and hydrogen chloride in presence of anhydrous aluminium chloride together with cuprous chloride (section 12.4.3). Benzene gives benzaldehyde :

\(\mathrm{C_6H_6} + \mathrm{CO} + \mathrm{HCl} \xrightarrow[\text{high pressure}]{\text{anhyd. } \mathrm{AlCl_3}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-CHO} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

The carbon monoxide and hydrogen chloride together behave as the formylating agent, so the reaction is the equivalent of a Friedel-Crafts acylation with formyl chloride, which is itself too unstable to be used.

answer:
Acetaldehyde is prepared from ethanoyl chloride by Rosenmund reduction. Hydrogen is passed over ethanoyl chloride in presence of palladium supported on barium sulfate, and the poisoned catalyst stops the reduction at the aldehyde (section 12.4.3).

\(\mathrm{CH_3-COCl} + \mathrm{H_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Pd/BaSO_4}} \mathrm{CH_3-CHO} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

The product \(\mathrm{CH_3-CHO}\) is ethanal, that is acetaldehyde.

Benzaldehyde is prepared from benzene by Gatterman-Koch formylation. Benzene is treated under high pressure with carbon monoxide and hydrogen chloride in presence of anhydrous aluminium chloride and cuprous chloride, and a \(\mathrm{-CHO}\) group takes the place of a ring hydrogen (section 12.4.3).

\(\mathrm{C_6H_6} + \mathrm{CO} + \mathrm{HCl} \xrightarrow[\text{high pressure}]{\text{anhyd. } \mathrm{AlCl_3}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-CHO} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

The product \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-CHO}\) is benzaldehyde.

Ethanenitrile is converted into ethanal by the Stephen reaction (section 12.4.3). The nitrile is reduced with stannous chloride and hydrochloric acid to the imine hydrochloride, and the imine hydrochloride is then hydrolysed with water to the aldehyde. Both carbon atoms of the nitrile are retained, so a two-carbon nitrile gives a two-carbon aldehyde.

Step 1 (reduction) :

\(\mathrm{CH_3-C{\equiv}N} + 2[\mathrm{H}] \xrightarrow{\mathrm{SnCl_2},\ \mathrm{HCl}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH{=}NH \cdot HCl}\)

Step 2 (acid hydrolysis) :

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH{=}NH \cdot HCl} + \mathrm{H_2O} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_3O^{\oplus}}} \mathrm{CH_3-CHO} + \mathrm{NH_4Cl}\)

The product \(\mathrm{CH_3-CHO}\) is ethanal.

answer:
**(D)** Propanone.

An alkyne adds water in presence of \(40\%\ \mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) and \(1\%\ \mathrm{HgSO_4}\) to give an aldehyde or a ketone (section 12.4.1). The addition follows Markovnikov's rule, so the \(\mathrm{-OH}\) goes to the carbon of the triple bond that already carries the alkyl group, and the enol first formed at once tautomerises to the carbonyl compound.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-C{\equiv}CH} + \mathrm{H_2O} \xrightarrow[40\%\ \mathrm{H_2SO_4}]{1\%\ \mathrm{HgSO_4}} [\mathrm{CH_3-C(OH){=}CH_2}]\)

\([\mathrm{CH_3-C(OH){=}CH_2}] \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3-CO-CH_3}\)

The carbon that receives the oxygen carries a methyl group on one side and a methyl group on the other, so the product has the \(\mathrm{{>}C{=}O}\) group between two alkyl groups; it is the ketone propanone (acetone). Ethyne is the only alkyne that gives an aldehyde on hydration, because it alone has no alkyl group on the carbon receiving the oxygen, so methanal, ethanal and propanal cannot be obtained from propyne.

**(C)** Acetone.

Ozonolysis breaks a carbon-carbon double bond completely: ozone first adds to give the ozonide, and the ozonide is then decomposed with zinc dust and water, the zinc dust being present to destroy the hydrogen peroxide formed so that the products are not oxidised further (section 12.4.1). Each doubly bonded carbon keeps the two groups it carried and gains the oxygen.

2,3-Dimethylbut-2-ene is \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2C{=}C(CH_3)_2}\). Both carbons of the double bond carry two methyl groups and no hydrogen, so both fragments are ketones and both are identical.

\(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2C{=}C(CH_3)_2} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{Zn}/\mathrm{H_2O}]{\mathrm{O_3}} 2\ \mathrm{CH_3-CO-CH_3}\)

Two molecules of propanone, that is acetone, are obtained and nothing else. An aldehyde could appear only if one of the doubly bonded carbons carried a hydrogen atom, and neither of them does, so acetaldehyde, propionaldehyde and butyraldehyde cannot be formed.

Step 1. Benzene reacts with ethanoyl chloride in presence of anhydrous aluminium chloride. This is Friedel-Crafts acylation: the acyl group replaces a hydrogen atom of the ring and hydrogen chloride is eliminated, which is how aromatic ketones are prepared from acyl chlorides (section 12.4.3).

\(\mathrm{C_6H_6} + \mathrm{CH_3-COCl} \xrightarrow[-\mathrm{HCl}]{\text{anhyd. } \mathrm{AlCl_3}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-CO-CH_3}\)

So \(\mathrm{A}\) is acetophenone (1-phenylethan-1-one), an aromatic ketone.

Step 2. Acetophenone is heated with zinc amalgam and concentrated hydrochloric acid. This is Clemmensen reduction, in which the carbonyl group is reduced to a methylene group, the oxygen being replaced by two hydrogen atoms and leaving as water (section 12.8.3). The water eliminated is the \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) shown in the given scheme.

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-CO-CH_3} + 4[\mathrm{H}] \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{Zn-Hg},\ \text{conc. } \mathrm{HCl}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-CH_2-CH_3} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

So \(\mathrm{B}\) is ethylbenzene.

\(\mathrm{A}\) = acetophenone, \(\mathrm{B}\) = ethylbenzene.

answer:
Wolf-Kishner reduction (section 12.8.3)

The carbonyl group of an aldehyde or a ketone is reduced to a methylene group when the compound is treated with hydrazine and the hydrazone so formed is then heated with sodium or potassium hydroxide in a high boiling solvent such as ethylene glycol. The oxygen of the carbonyl group is replaced by two hydrogen atoms.

Step 1. The carbonyl compound and hydrazine lose a molecule of water to give the hydrazone :

\(\mathrm{{>}C{=}O} + \mathrm{NH_2-NH_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{{>}C{=}N-NH_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

Step 2. The hydrazone, heated with alkali in ethylene glycol, loses nitrogen :

\(\mathrm{{>}C{=}N-NH_2} \xrightarrow[\text{ethylene glycol},\ \Delta]{\mathrm{KOH}} \mathrm{{>}CH_2} + \mathrm{N_2}\)

For example, propanone gives propane :

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CO-CH_3} \xrightarrow[\text{ii. } \mathrm{KOH}/\text{ethylene glycol},\ \Delta]{\text{i. } \mathrm{NH_2-NH_2}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_3} + \mathrm{N_2}\)

The reaction is used where the acidic conditions of Clemmensen reduction cannot be employed, and it gives straight chain alkyl benzenes that Friedel-Crafts alkylation cannot.

Preparation of propanone from ethanoyl chloride and dimethyl cadmium

Dialkyl cadmium is obtained by treating cadmium chloride with a Grignard reagent, and it converts an acyl chloride into a ketone (section 12.4.3) :

\(2\ \mathrm{CH_3-MgX} + \mathrm{CdCl_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{(CH_3)_2Cd} + 2\ \mathrm{Mg(X)Cl}\)

\(2\ \mathrm{CH_3-COCl} + \mathrm{(CH_3)_2Cd} \longrightarrow 2\ \mathrm{CH_3-CO-CH_3} + \mathrm{CdCl_2}\)

The ketone obtained from ethanoyl chloride and dimethyl cadmium is propanone (acetone).

answer:
Aldol condensation (section 12.8.2 g)

An aldehyde or a ketone that has at least one \(\alpha\)-hydrogen atom adds to a second molecule of itself in presence of dilute alkali. The dilute alkali removes an \(\alpha\)-hydrogen from one molecule to give a carbanion, and this carbanion attacks the carbonyl carbon of the second molecule. The product of the addition is a \(\beta\)-hydroxy carbonyl compound, called an aldol when it comes from an aldehyde and a ketol when it comes from a ketone. On warming, the aldol loses a molecule of water across the \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) positions to give an \(\alpha,\beta\)-unsaturated carbonyl compound.

Step 1, addition :

\(2\ \mathrm{CH_3-CHO} \xrightarrow{\text{dil. NaOH}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH(OH)-CH_2-CHO}\)

(3-hydroxybutanal, an aldol)

Step 2, elimination :

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(OH)-CH_2-CHO} \xrightarrow[-\mathrm{H_2O}]{\Delta} \mathrm{CH_3-CH{=}CH-CHO}\)

(but-2-enal)

The name condensation is given because the two molecules join with the loss of a small molecule, water. An aldehyde with no \(\alpha\)-hydrogen atom, such as methanal or benzaldehyde, cannot give the reaction; it gives the Cannizzaro reaction instead. When two different carbonyl compounds each having \(\alpha\)-hydrogen atoms are used, a mixture of four products is obtained, and the reaction is then called a cross aldol condensation.

answer:
Mechanism of the aldol addition reaction (section 12.8.2 g)

Ethanal is taken as the example. It has three \(\alpha\)-hydrogen atoms, and an \(\alpha\)-hydrogen is acidic because the carbanion left behind is stabilised by the neighbouring carbonyl group.

Step 1. The hydroxide ion of the dilute alkali removes an \(\alpha\)-hydrogen atom from one molecule of ethanal, giving a carbanion :

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CHO} + \mathrm{OH^{\ominus}} \longrightarrow [\mathrm{{}^{\ominus}CH_2-CHO}] + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

The carbanion is resonance stabilised, the negative charge being shared between the \(\alpha\)-carbon and the oxygen :

\([\mathrm{{}^{\ominus}CH_2-CHO}] \longleftrightarrow [\mathrm{CH_2{=}CH-O^{\ominus}}]\)

Step 2. The carbanion acts as the nucleophile and attacks the positively polarised carbonyl carbon of a second molecule of ethanal, and the \(\pi\) electrons of that carbonyl group shift to oxygen. An alkoxide ion is formed :

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CHO} + [\mathrm{{}^{\ominus}CH_2-CHO}] \longrightarrow [\mathrm{CH_3-CH(O^{\ominus})-CH_2-CHO}]\)

Step 3. The alkoxide ion takes a proton from water, which also regenerates the hydroxide ion, so the alkali acts as a catalyst :

\([\mathrm{CH_3-CH(O^{\ominus})-CH_2-CHO}] + \mathrm{H_2O} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3-CH(OH)-CH_2-CHO} + \mathrm{OH^{\ominus}}\)

The product is 3-hydroxybutanal, the aldol. The whole change is therefore a nucleophilic addition of one molecule of the aldehyde across the carbonyl group of another.

Two uses of carboxylic acids

1. Acetic acid is the key ingredient of vinegar, and is used in food as a preservative and a flavouring agent.

2. The sodium and potassium salts of the higher fatty acids are soaps, and are obtained by the alkaline hydrolysis of the esters of those acids, that is by saponification.

answer:
Self oxidation and reduction of an aldehyde is the Cannizzaro reaction (section 12.8.2 h).

An aldehyde that has no \(\alpha\)-hydrogen atom cannot give the aldol reaction. On heating with concentrated alkali such an aldehyde undergoes self oxidation and reduction, that is a disproportionation: one molecule of the aldehyde is reduced to the corresponding alcohol while at the same time a second molecule is oxidised to the salt of the carboxylic acid.

\(2\ \mathrm{R-CHO} + \mathrm{NaOH}\ (\text{conc.}) \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{R-CH_2OH} + \mathrm{R-COONa}\)

Suitable example. Methanal has no \(\alpha\)-hydrogen atom, and with 50 per cent sodium hydroxide it gives methanol and sodium formate :

\(2\ \mathrm{H-CHO} + \mathrm{NaOH} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{CH_3-OH} + \mathrm{H-COONa}\)

The carbon of one molecule goes from the aldehyde level down to the alcohol level, a reduction, and the carbon of the other goes from the aldehyde level up to the carboxylate level, an oxidation. Both changes happen to the same substance in the same reaction, which is why it is called a self oxidation and reduction reaction. Benzaldehyde behaves in the same way and gives benzyl alcohol and sodium benzoate.

answer:
**(B)** Butan-2-ol, \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(OH)-CH_2-CH_3}\).

The compound shown is \(\mathrm{C_2H_5-CO-CH_3}\), butan-2-one. Hydrogen in presence of a nickel catalyst on heating is a catalytic reduction of the carbonyl group: the two hydrogen atoms add across the \(\mathrm{{>}C{=}O}\) bond, one to carbon and one to oxygen, so a ketone gives a secondary alcohol and the carbon skeleton is unchanged.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CO-CH_3} + \mathrm{H_2} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{Ni}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH(OH)-CH_3}\)

The four carbon atoms are retained and the oxygen is retained, so the product is butan-2-ol, in which the \(\mathrm{-OH}\) group sits on the carbon that carried the \(\mathrm{{>}C{=}O}\) group. Butan-1-ol would require the oxygen to move to the end of the chain, butane would require the oxygen to be removed altogether, which needs Clemmensen or Wolf-Kishner conditions, and butanoic acid would require an oxidation, which hydrogen cannot bring about.

answer:
**(B)** \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH{=}CH-CH_2-CH_2-OH}\), pent-3-en-1-ol.

The compound shown is \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH{=}CH-CH_2-CHO}\), pent-3-enal. Lithium aluminium hydride followed by acid work-up reduces the carbonyl group of an aldehyde to a primary alcohol; it delivers hydride to the carbonyl carbon, and the alkoxide formed is then protonated in the second step by \(\mathrm{H_3O^{\oplus}}\).

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH{=}CH-CH_2-CHO} \xrightarrow[\text{ii. } \mathrm{H_3O^{\oplus}}]{\text{i. } \mathrm{LiAlH_4}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH{=}CH-CH_2-CH_2-OH}\)

An isolated carbon-carbon double bond is not polar and offers no electrophilic carbon for hydride to attack, so lithium aluminium hydride leaves it untouched. The double bond therefore survives and stays at the same place in the chain, and the five carbon atoms are retained. The product is pent-3-en-1-ol.

A saturated alcohol would require the double bond to be reduced as well, which \(\mathrm{LiAlH_4}\) does not do, and either of the two acids would require the aldehyde to be oxidised, which a reducing agent cannot bring about.

Aldol condensation of ethanal (section 12.8.2 g)

Ethanal has three \(\alpha\)-hydrogen atoms, so it undergoes aldol condensation with dilute alkali. The reaction takes place in two stages.

Stage 1, aldol addition. Dilute sodium hydroxide removes an \(\alpha\)-hydrogen atom from one molecule of ethanal to give a carbanion, and the carbanion attacks the carbonyl carbon of a second molecule of ethanal. The product is the \(\beta\)-hydroxy aldehyde :

\(2\ \mathrm{CH_3-CHO} \xrightarrow{\text{dil. NaOH}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH(OH)-CH_2-CHO}\)

The product \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(OH)-CH_2-CHO}\) is 3-hydroxybutanal, and it is called an aldol because it carries both an aldehyde group and an alcohol group.

Stage 2, dehydration. On warming, the aldol loses a molecule of water, the \(\mathrm{-OH}\) going from the \(\beta\)-carbon and a hydrogen atom from the \(\alpha\)-carbon, so a double bond appears between them :

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(OH)-CH_2-CHO} \xrightarrow[-\mathrm{H_2O}]{\Delta} \mathrm{CH_3-CH{=}CH-CHO}\)

The final product is but-2-enal, an \(\alpha,\beta\)-unsaturated aldehyde. Two molecules of the two-carbon ethanal have joined to give a four-carbon chain, and the loss of water in the second stage is what makes the reaction a condensation.

answer:
Cannizzaro reaction of benzaldehyde (section 12.8.2 h)

Benzaldehyde, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-CHO}\), has its \(\mathrm{-CHO}\) group attached directly to the ring, so there is no \(\alpha\)-carbon and therefore no \(\alpha\)-hydrogen atom. It cannot give the aldol reaction. On heating with concentrated alkali it undergoes self oxidation and reduction, a disproportionation in which one molecule is reduced and another is oxidised.

\(2\ \mathrm{C_6H_5-CHO} + \mathrm{NaOH}\ (\text{conc.}) \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{C_6H_5-CH_2OH} + \mathrm{C_6H_5-COONa}\)

One molecule of benzaldehyde is reduced to benzyl alcohol, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-CH_2OH}\), and the second molecule is oxidised to sodium benzoate, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-COONa}\). On acidification of the reaction mixture the sodium benzoate gives free benzoic acid :

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-COONa} + \mathrm{HCl} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5-COOH} + \mathrm{NaCl}\)

The absence of an \(\alpha\)-hydrogen atom is the condition for the reaction, which is why benzaldehyde gives it and ethanal does not.

answer:
The reagents used in Clemmensen reduction are zinc amalgam, that is zinc treated with mercury and written \(\mathrm{Zn-Hg}\), and concentrated hydrochloric acid.

Heating an aldehyde or a ketone with this pair reduces the carbonyl group to a methylene group; the oxygen atom is replaced by two hydrogen atoms and is removed as water (section 12.8.3).

\(\mathrm{{>}C{=}O} + 4[\mathrm{H}] \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{Zn-Hg},\ \text{conc. } \mathrm{HCl}} \mathrm{{>}CH_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

For example, propanone gives propane :

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CO-CH_3} + 4[\mathrm{H}] \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{Zn-Hg},\ \text{conc. } \mathrm{HCl}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_3} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

Because the medium is strongly acidic, a compound that cannot withstand acid is reduced by the Wolf-Kishner method instead, which uses hydrazine and alkali and brings about the same change.

Classification of aliphatic ketones (section 12.2.2)

An aliphatic ketone has its \(\mathrm{{>}C{=}O}\) group attached to two alkyl groups, \(\mathrm{R-CO-R'}\). They are classified according to whether those two alkyl groups are the same or different.

i. Simple or symmetrical ketones. Both the alkyl groups bonded to the carbonyl carbon are identical.
Example : \(\mathrm{CH_3-CO-CH_3}\), propanone (dimethyl ketone, acetone).

ii. Mixed or unsymmetrical ketones. The two alkyl groups bonded to the carbonyl carbon are different.
Example : \(\mathrm{CH_3-CO-C_2H_5}\), butan-2-one (ethyl methyl ketone).

Action of sodium hypoiodite on acetone

Acetone is a methyl ketone, that is it carries a \(\mathrm{CH_3-CO-}\) group, so it gives the haloform reaction (section 12.8.2 f). The reagent sodium hypoiodite is produced in situ from iodine and sodium hydroxide. The methyl group attached to the carbonyl carbon is converted into iodoform, and the rest of the molecule is left as the sodium salt of the acid having one carbon atom less than the ketone.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CO-CH_3} + 3\ \mathrm{NaOI} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CHI_3}\downarrow + \mathrm{CH_3-COONa} + 2\ \mathrm{NaOH}\)

What is observed is a yellow precipitate of iodoform, \(\mathrm{CHI_3}\), and the other product is sodium acetate. The yellow precipitate is the test for the \(\mathrm{CH_3-CO-}\) group; a ketone that is not a methyl ketone gives no precipitate.

Racemic mixture. A racemic mixture is a mixture that contains the two enantiomers of a chiral compound in equal, that is equimolar, proportions. The rotation of the plane of polarised light produced by one enantiomer is exactly equal and opposite to that produced by the other, so the two cancel and the mixture as a whole is optically inactive. This cancellation is called external compensation, and such a mixture is written with the prefix \((\pm)\) or dl.

IUPAC name. The compound whose name is asked is the aldehyde \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH(CH_3)-CHO}\).

The principal functional group is \(\mathrm{-CHO}\), so its carbon must be numbered 1 and the parent chain must contain it. The longest chain through that carbon has four carbon atoms, so the parent is butanal, and a methyl group is attached to C-2.

IUPAC name : 2-methylbutanal.

C-2 of this molecule carries four different groups, namely \(\mathrm{-H}\), \(\mathrm{-CH_3}\), \(\mathrm{-C_2H_5}\) and \(\mathrm{-CHO}\), so it is a chiral carbon. 2-Methylbutanal therefore exists as a pair of enantiomers, and an equimolar mixture of those two is a racemic mixture of the kind defined above.

answer:
**(B)** Acetophenone.

Acetophenone, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-CO-CH_3}\), is an aromatic ketone that has the smell of pistachio, and it is used to give that flavour to ice cream.

The other three compounds named are used elsewhere. Vanillin is the aldehyde responsible for the flavour of vanilla; muscone is a ketone with a musky aroma and is used in perfumes; butyraldehyde has a buttery odour and is used in margarine and food.

i. Acetic acid into acetic anhydride

A better yield of an acid anhydride is obtained by heating the sodium salt of the acid with the acyl chloride (section 12.9.5), so acetic acid is first converted into each of those two.

Preparation of the acyl chloride, with thionyl chloride :

\(\mathrm{CH_3-COOH} + \mathrm{SOCl_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3-COCl} + \mathrm{SO_2} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

Preparation of the sodium salt, with sodium hydroxide :

\(\mathrm{CH_3-COOH} + \mathrm{NaOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3-COONa} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

The two are then heated together :

\(\mathrm{CH_3-COONa} + \mathrm{CH_3-COCl} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{(CH_3CO)_2O} + \mathrm{NaCl}\)

The product \(\mathrm{(CH_3CO)_2O}\) is acetic anhydride.

ii. Acetic acid into ethyl alcohol

A carboxylic acid is reduced to the primary alcohol by a powerful reducing agent such as lithium aluminium hydride in dry ether (section 12.9.7). Both carbon atoms are retained, so the two-carbon acid gives the two-carbon alcohol.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-COOH} + 4[\mathrm{H}] \xrightarrow{\mathrm{LiAlH_4}/\text{dry ether}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-OH} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

The product \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-OH}\) is ethyl alcohol.

An acid anhydride is obtained in good yield by heating the sodium salt of the acid with the corresponding acyl chloride (section 12.9.5). Starting from acetic acid, both of those are first prepared from the acid itself.

Step 1. Acetic acid with thionyl chloride gives ethanoyl chloride :

\(\mathrm{CH_3-COOH} + \mathrm{SOCl_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3-COCl} + \mathrm{SO_2} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

Step 2. Acetic acid with sodium hydroxide gives sodium acetate :

\(\mathrm{CH_3-COOH} + \mathrm{NaOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3-COONa} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

Step 3. Sodium acetate heated with ethanoyl chloride gives acetic anhydride :

\(\mathrm{CH_3-COONa} + \mathrm{CH_3-COCl} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{CH_3-CO-O-CO-CH_3} + \mathrm{NaCl}\)

Counting the atoms on the two sides of the third equation, there are two ethanoyl groups, one oxygen bridging them, one sodium and one chlorine on each side, so the equation is balanced as written. The product \(\mathrm{CH_3-CO-O-CO-CH_3}\), that is \(\mathrm{(CH_3CO)_2O}\), is acetic anhydride.

Fischer esterification is the formation of an ester from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol, heated together in presence of a small quantity of concentrated sulfuric acid, which acts as the catalyst and also removes the water formed.

\(\mathrm{R-COOH} + \mathrm{R'-OH} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{conc. } \mathrm{H_2SO_4}} \mathrm{R-COOR'} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

For example, acetic acid and ethyl alcohol give ethyl acetate :

\(\mathrm{CH_3-COOH} + \mathrm{C_2H_5-OH} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{conc. } \mathrm{H_2SO_4}} \mathrm{CH_3-COOC_2H_5} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

The reaction is reversible, so the ester is obtained in good yield only when the water is removed as it is formed or one of the reactants is taken in excess. The oxygen atom of the ester link comes from the alcohol, the \(\mathrm{-OH}\) of the acid being the part that leaves with the hydrogen of the alcohol as water.

A carboxylic acid that has an \(\alpha\)-hydrogen atom reacts with chlorine or bromine in presence of a small amount of red phosphorus, and a halogen atom takes the place of a hydrogen atom on the \(\alpha\)-carbon. This is the Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky reaction.

\(\mathrm{R-CH_2-COOH} + \mathrm{X_2} \xrightarrow{\text{red P}} \mathrm{R-CHX-COOH} + \mathrm{HX}\)

For example, acetic acid with chlorine gives chloroacetic acid :

\(\mathrm{CH_3-COOH} + \mathrm{Cl_2} \xrightarrow{\text{red P}} \mathrm{Cl-CH_2-COOH} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

With more of the halogen the substitution goes further, giving dichloroacetic acid and then trichloroacetic acid. Only the \(\alpha\)-hydrogen is replaced, so an acid that has none, such as benzoic acid or trimethylacetic acid, does not give this reaction. The \(\alpha\)-halo acids so obtained are useful because the halogen can afterwards be replaced by other groups.

Ethyl alcohol is converted into ethyl acetate by esterification. It is heated with ethanoic acid in presence of a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid, which catalyses the reaction and takes up the water formed.

\(\mathrm{C_2H_5-OH} + \mathrm{CH_3-COOH} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{conc. } \mathrm{H_2SO_4}} \mathrm{CH_3-COOC_2H_5} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

The product \(\mathrm{CH_3-COOC_2H_5}\) is ethyl acetate, that is ethyl ethanoate. The reaction is reversible, so the ester is distilled off as it forms, or one reactant is taken in excess, to drive it to completion.

Soda lime is a mixture of sodium hydroxide and calcium oxide. Sodium acetate heated with soda lime undergoes decarboxylation (section 12.9.6): the carboxyl group is lost as carbonate and the hydrocarbon that remains has one carbon atom less than the acid from which the salt was made.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-COONa} + \mathrm{NaOH} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{CaO}} \mathrm{CH_4} + \mathrm{Na_2CO_3}\)

The action of soda lime on sodium acetate is therefore to give methane. Sodium acetate has two carbon atoms and methane has one, which is the loss of the carboxyl carbon as carbonate; the calcium oxide is present to keep the sodium hydroxide dry and to make it easier to handle.

Trichloroacetic acid is the strongest of the acids named.

The strength of a carboxylic acid is decided by how well the carboxylate ion left after the loss of the proton is stabilised. Chlorine is strongly electronegative and exerts an electron withdrawing inductive effect. That effect pulls the negative charge of the carboxylate ion away from the carboxyl group and spreads it over the molecule, so the conjugate base is stabilised and the acid becomes stronger. The more chlorine atoms there are on the \(\alpha\)-carbon, the greater the withdrawal and the stronger the acid (Table 12.9) :

\(\mathrm{CH_3-COOH}\), \(\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a} = 4.76\), no chlorine atom
\(\mathrm{Cl-CH_2-COOH}\), \(\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a} = 2.86\), one chlorine atom
\(\mathrm{Cl_2CH-COOH}\), \(\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a} = 1.26\), two chlorine atoms
\(\mathrm{Cl_3C-COOH}\), \(\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a} = 0.6\), three chlorine atoms

The lower the \(\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a}\) the stronger the acid, so the order of increasing acid strength is acetic acid, then dichloroacetic acid, then trichloroacetic acid, and trichloroacetic acid is the strongest.

The same compound, trichloroacetic acid, is printed as two of the four alternatives of this question, so the three distinct compounds offered are acetic acid, dichloroacetic acid and trichloroacetic acid, and no single alternative can be marked as the answer.

answer:
**(D)** p-Aminophenol.

All four compounds are phenols, and each ionises the same \(\mathrm{O-H}\) bond, so their strengths differ only through what the substituent does to the phenoxide ion left behind. An electron withdrawing group spreads the negative charge of the phenoxide, stabilises it and makes the acid stronger; an electron donating group pushes electron density towards the already negatively charged oxygen, destabilises the phenoxide and makes the acid weaker.

Taking the four in turn :

p-Nitrophenol. The nitro group is strongly electron withdrawing by both the inductive and the resonance effect, so it is the strongest acid of the four.

p-Chlorophenol. Chlorine is electronegative and withdraws electrons inductively, so it too is a stronger acid than phenol itself.

p-Cresol. The methyl group is electron donating, so the acid is weaker than phenol.

p-Aminophenol. The amino group is also electron donating, and it donates a lone pair of nitrogen into the ring by resonance as well as by the inductive effect. That is a stronger donation than the methyl group can provide, so the phenoxide ion is destabilised most and the acid is the weakest of the four.

Arranged in decreasing order of acid strength : p-nitrophenol, p-chlorophenol, p-cresol, p-aminophenol. The weakest is therefore p-aminophenol.

Benzoic acid is the strongest acid of the four printed.

The four compounds are benzoic acid and three substituted benzoic acids: 3-hydroxybenzoic acid, 2-aminobenzoic acid and 4-methoxybenzoic acid. Their strengths differ through what the substituent does to the carboxylate ion left after the proton is lost. An electron withdrawing group spreads that negative charge and stabilises the conjugate base, so the acid becomes stronger; an electron donating group intensifies the charge and destabilises the conjugate base, so the acid becomes weaker.

The chapter states which groups are which: electron withdrawing groups such as \(\mathrm{-Cl}\), \(\mathrm{-CN}\) and \(\mathrm{-NO_2}\) increase the acidity of substituted benzoic acids, while electron donating groups such as \(\mathrm{-CH_3}\), \(\mathrm{-OH}\), \(\mathrm{-OCH_3}\) and \(\mathrm{-NH_2}\) decrease it.

Applying that classification to the three substituted acids :

\(\mathrm{-OH}\) is electron donating, so 3-hydroxybenzoic acid is weaker than benzoic acid.
\(\mathrm{-NH_2}\) is electron donating, so 2-aminobenzoic acid is weaker than benzoic acid.
\(\mathrm{-OCH_3}\) is electron donating, so 4-methoxybenzoic acid is weaker than benzoic acid.

Every substituent present is one that the chapter names as acidity-decreasing, so each of the three substituted acids is weaker than the parent. The unsubstituted acid, benzoic acid, is left as the strongest of the four.

Dry ice is solid carbon dioxide. Ethanoic acid is prepared from it by the Grignard route (section 12.5.6).

Step 1. Methylmagnesium bromide, prepared from methyl bromide and magnesium, is taken in dry ether and added to solid carbon dioxide. The carbon of the carbon dioxide becomes the carboxyl carbon, and the magnesium salt of the acid is formed :

\(\mathrm{CH_3-MgBr} + \mathrm{O{=}C{=}O} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \mathrm{CH_3-COOMgBr}\)

Step 2. The complex is hydrolysed with dilute hydrochloric acid, which liberates the free acid :

\(\mathrm{CH_3-COOMgBr} \xrightarrow{\text{dil. HCl}} \mathrm{CH_3-COOH} + \mathrm{Mg(OH)Br}\)

The product \(\mathrm{CH_3-COOH}\) is ethanoic acid. The acid obtained has one carbon atom more than the alkyl halide from which the Grignard reagent was made, that carbon coming from the carbon dioxide. Dry ice serves twice over here, as the reagent that supplies the carboxyl carbon and, subliming at a low temperature, as the cooling agent that keeps this strongly exothermic reaction cold.

Carbolic acid is the trivial name of phenol.

Preparation of carbolic acid from benzene sulphonic acid

Step 1. Benzene sulphonic acid is neutralised with sodium hydroxide to give sodium benzene sulphonate :

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-SO_3H} + \mathrm{NaOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5-SO_3Na} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

Step 2. The salt is fused with solid sodium hydroxide at 573 K, when the sulphonate group is replaced and sodium phenoxide is obtained :

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-SO_3Na} + 2\ \mathrm{NaOH} \xrightarrow{573\ \mathrm{K}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-ONa} + \mathrm{Na_2SO_3} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

Step 3. The phenoxide is treated with a dilute acid, which liberates free phenol :

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-ONa} + \mathrm{HCl} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5-OH} + \mathrm{NaCl}\)

The product \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-OH}\) is phenol, that is carbolic acid.

Action of neutral ferric chloride on phenol

Phenol reacts with neutral ferric chloride solution to give a deep violet colouration, which is the colour of the ferric phenoxide complex formed. What is observed is the appearance of that violet colour, and it is the standard test for a phenolic \(\mathrm{-OH}\) group.

\(3\ \mathrm{C_6H_5-OH} + \mathrm{FeCl_3} \longrightarrow \mathrm{(C_6H_5-O)_3Fe} + 3\ \mathrm{HCl}\)

An alkene is oxidised by potassium permanganate in dilute sulfuric acid, and the oxidation cleaves the carbon-carbon double bond and converts each of the two doubly bonded carbon atoms into a carboxyl group (section 12.5.5).

In cyclohexene both carbons of the \(\mathrm{C{=}C}\) bond are part of the ring, so cleaving that bond opens the ring instead of splitting the molecule in two. A single open chain is left, carrying a \(\mathrm{-COOH}\) group at each of its two ends.

\(\mathrm{C_6H_{10}} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{KMnO_4}/\text{dil. } \mathrm{H_2SO_4}} \mathrm{HOOC-CH_2-CH_2-CH_2-CH_2-COOH}\)

Counting the carbon atoms, cyclohexene has six and the product has six, the two that carried the double bond having become the two carboxyl carbons and the remaining four forming the \(\mathrm{-(CH_2)_4-}\) chain between them. The product \(\mathrm{HOOC-(CH_2)_4-COOH}\) is hexanedioic acid, known by its common name adipic acid.

Commercial method for the preparation of glucose

Glucose is obtained commercially by the hydrolysis of starch. Starch is boiled with dilute sulfuric acid at 393 K under a pressure of 2 to 3 atmospheres. Every glycosidic linkage of the polysaccharide is broken, and since starch is built entirely of glucose units, glucose alone is obtained :

\(\mathrm{(C_6H_{10}O_5)_n} + n\ \mathrm{H_2O} \xrightarrow[2-3\ \text{atm}]{\text{dil. } \mathrm{H_2SO_4},\ 393\ \mathrm{K}} n\ \mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6}\)

Structure of adipic acid

Adipic acid is a straight chain dicarboxylic acid of six carbon atoms, carrying a \(\mathrm{-COOH}\) group at each end of the chain :

\(\mathrm{HOOC-CH_2-CH_2-CH_2-CH_2-COOH}\)

which is written more briefly as \(\mathrm{HOOC-(CH_2)_4-COOH}\). Its IUPAC name is hexanedioic acid, the six carbon atoms being the four of the \(\mathrm{-(CH_2)_4-}\) chain together with the two carboxyl carbons.

Ethylamine has two carbon atoms and methyl iodide has one, so the chain must first be lengthened by one carbon atom. The nitrile group supplies that carbon.

Step 1. Methyl iodide is heated with alcoholic potassium cyanide. The cyanide ion attacks through its carbon atom, so the nitrile is obtained :

\(\mathrm{CH_3-I} + \mathrm{KCN} \xrightarrow{\text{alcoholic}} \mathrm{CH_3-C{\equiv}N} + \mathrm{KI}\)

The product \(\mathrm{CH_3-C{\equiv}N}\) is ethanenitrile, and it has two carbon atoms.

Step 2. The nitrile is reduced with lithium aluminium hydride in dry ether, or with sodium and ethyl alcohol. Four hydrogen atoms add across the triple bond of the \(\mathrm{-C{\equiv}N}\) group, which becomes \(\mathrm{-CH_2-NH_2}\) :

\(\mathrm{CH_3-C{\equiv}N} + 4[\mathrm{H}] \xrightarrow{\mathrm{LiAlH_4}/\text{dry ether}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-NH_2}\)

The product \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-NH_2}\) is ethylamine, a primary amine with the same number of carbon atoms as the nitrile. Alcoholic potassium cyanide is used at the first step and not silver cyanide, because silver cyanide would attack through nitrogen and give the isocyanide, which on reduction gives a secondary amine instead.
